More than a drink

How to prepare yerba mate.

Making mate for the first time? Start with the ritual, not just the recipe. Learn how South Americans prepare, share and choose yerba mate.

The ritual first

Mate is prepared slowly.

Yerba mate is not prepared like a tea bag in a mug. Traditionally, mate is made with loose yerba leaves placed inside a gourd, then sipped through a filtered metal straw called a bombilla.

In many parts of South America, especially Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and southern Brazil, mate is part of everyday life. People drink it in the morning, while studying, at work, in parks, during road trips, or when gathering with friends and family.

But mate is not only about energy or taste. It is also about rhythm. You prepare it slowly, refill it many times, and share it one pour at a time. The ritual invites people to pause, talk, listen and be present.

The traditional way

What you need before you start.

A traditional mate setup is simple, but each part has a role.

01

Yerba mate

The dried leaves used to make the drink. Different yerba brands can taste smooth, grassy, smoky, bitter or strong.

02

Mate gourd

The cup where the yerba is placed. It can be made from calabash, wood, stainless steel or other materials.

03

Bombilla

The filtered metal straw. It lets you drink the infusion while keeping the leaves inside the gourd.

04

Hot water

Mate is prepared with hot water, but not boiling water. Around 75–80°C helps protect the flavour.

Step by step

How to prepare your first mate.

Keep the montañita — the small yerba “mountain” — intact, pour water into the same side, and try not to move the bombilla once it is placed.

How South Americans drink mate

One cebador, one circle, one rhythm.

In South America, mate can be personal or social. Some people drink mate alone while working, studying or starting the day. It becomes a quiet habit, almost like a companion.

When mate is shared, it has its own rhythm. Usually, one person prepares and pours the mate. This person is often called the cebador or cebadora — the one who serves the mate.

The cebador is not usually changed in the middle. They take care of the water, the gourd and the flow of the circle.

The gourd is passed to one person at a time. You drink, enjoy the moment, then return it to the cebador, who refills it and passes it to the next person.

In a way, the bombilla becomes your little microphone. While you hold the mate, you have your moment — to talk, listen, laugh, or simply enjoy the pause.

Mate is often shared with something sweet, like pastries, biscuits or desserts, making it part of a relaxed conversation rather than a rushed drink.

There is also a small cultural detail: you usually only say “thank you” when you do not want any more mate. If you say thank you too early, the cebador may understand that you are finished.

This may feel unusual to people who are new to mate, but culturally it represents trust, closeness and hospitality. Sharing mate is less about serving a drink and more about sharing time.

Beginner notes

What beginners should know.

Do not use boiling water.

Boiling water can make mate taste too bitter and may damage the yerba. Aim for around 75–80°C.

Do not stir with the bombilla.

The bombilla is not a spoon. Moving it too much can block the filter and disturb the yerba.

Do not flood the whole gourd.

Pour water into the same lower side and refill slowly, keeping the montañita intact.

The flavour changes over time.

The first few pours can taste stronger. As you keep refilling, the flavour becomes softer and smoother.
